title: New York City Council Stated Meeting: 'City of Yes for Housing Opportunity' Zoning Reform, Infrastructure Capital Budget, & Roll Call Vote
context: Verbatim-reconstructed high-stakes municipal legislative deliberation from the New York City Council Stated Meeting and Committee on Land Use / Subcommittee on Zoning and Franchises. Debates the historic 'City of Yes for Housing Opportunity' citywide zoning text amendment, evaluating the Universal Affordability Preference (UAP) floor area ratio bonuses, the elimination of mandatory off-street parking minimums across outer-borough transit zones, neighborhood infrastructure absorption capacity (stormwater sewers, school seats, transit crowding), community board advisory rejections, and the negotiation of a landmark $5.0 billion municipal capital infrastructure investment commitment package.

metadata.matter: LU 0118-2024 / City of Yes for Housing Opportunity (Zoning Text Amendment)
metadata.capital_package: $5.0 Billion Capital Infrastructure & Tenant Protection Agreement

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: The Stated Meeting of the New York City Council will come to order. Today, the Council confronts the single greatest crisis threatening the working-class families of our city: our severe, historic housing shortage. New York City's rental vacancy rate has plunged to an alarming 1.4 percent—the lowest level recorded since 1968. For apartments renting under $1,500 a month, the vacancy rate is an astonishing 0.39 percent. We face a choice between the status quo of escalating rents and displacement or taking bold, citywide legislative action through the 'City of Yes for Housing Opportunity' zoning text amendment. However, this Council will not approve any zoning change without binding guarantees of deeply affordable housing and substantial capital investments in neighborhood infrastructure.

turns.speaker: Kevin Riley
turns.text: As Chair of the Subcommittee on Zoning and Franchises, I present the committee report. The Administration's original proposal sought to generate approximately 109,000 new homes across all five boroughs over 15 years. A central pillar is the Universal Affordability Preference, or UAP, which allows residential developments to build 20 percent more housing floor area ratio, provided that additional 20 percent is permanently income-restricted affordable housing at an average of 60 percent of Area Median Income. This replaces the outdated Voluntary Inclusionary Housing program and incentivizes affordable units in high-opportunity neighborhoods where affordable development has been virtually non-existent.

turns.speaker: Rafael Salamanca Jr.
turns.text: As Chair of the Land Use Committee, representing the South Bronx, I have made our position clear to City Planning from day one: our communities have shouldered an unfair share of housing development while affluent neighborhoods have downzoned themselves behind exclusionary rules. If we approve citywide zoning changes, the burden of growth must be shared equitably across every community district in all five boroughs. We cannot allow developers to build market-rate luxury towers with token affordability while our subway lines and sewer mains overflow.

turns.speaker: Dan Garodnick
turns.text: Thank you, Speaker Adams and Chairs Salamanca and Riley. As Chair of the City Planning Commission, I want to emphasize that New York City's 1961 Zoning Resolution was designed for an automobile-dominated, post-war era that artificially capped housing growth. Over the last decade, our city added 800,000 jobs but built only 200,000 homes. UAP unlocks capacity for affordable homes directly over existing transit nodes and commercial corridors without spending scarce municipal subsidy dollars on market-rate land acquisition. Every neighborhood must contribute to solving this crisis.

turns.speaker: Pierina Sanchez
turns.text: As Housing and Buildings Chair representing District 14 in the West Bronx, where working families are battling evictions and severe overcrowding, I support the intent of UAP, but the affordability targets must be deepened. Setting UAP at 60 percent of Area Median Income means an individual must earn $65,000 a year to qualify, yet the median income in my district is $32,000. Unless UAP is paired with City-subsidized Extremely Low Income and Very Low Income affordability tiers at 30 percent AMI, these units will remain out of reach for the very families facing eviction.

turns.speaker: Tiffany Cabán
turns.text: The Progressive Caucus shares these grave concerns. Private developers claim that upzoning through zoning text deregulation automatically trickles down to create affordability, but real-world experience demonstrates that market-rate supply without rent stabilization and strict tenant protections accelerates tenant harassment and neighborhood gentrification. We cannot rely on private market developer bonuses as our primary affordable housing strategy.

turns.speaker: Keith Powers
turns.text: As Majority Leader representing Manhattan, I can attest that neighborhoods like mine must build more housing. For decades, Manhattan community districts have used restrictive historic zoning overlays to block new construction, driving rents through the roof. The Universal Affordability Preference creates a citywide standard where every neighborhood contributes its fair share of permanently affordable housing.

turns.speaker: Joseph Borelli
turns.text: On behalf of the Minority Conference, we strongly reject the premise that stripping local communities of zoning control will fix housing affordability. This proposal is a developer-driven giveaway that dismantles the low-density character of Staten Island, Southern Brooklyn, and Eastern Queens. Imposing higher floor-area ratios and apartment buildings into quiet single-family neighborhoods will destroy community character without lowering housing costs.

turns.speaker: Vickie Paladino
turns.text: Councilman Borelli is 100 percent right. In District 19 in Northeast Queens, our infrastructure is already failing. Our schools are overcrowded, our roads are jammed, and storm drains back up during every thunderstorm. Flooding our quiet residential neighborhoods with multi-family developments through unilateral city hall edicts is an assault on suburban homeowners.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: Round 1 outlines the core debate over the Universal Affordability Preference. In Round 2, we confront the most contentious provision of this proposal: the elimination of mandatory off-street parking minimums.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: We begin Round 2 on parking mandates and transit-oriented development. Under the Department of City Planning's proposal, mandatory off-street parking minimums would be completely eliminated for all new residential developments citywide. Proponents argue that parking mandates inflate housing construction costs by up to $60,000 to $100,000 per underground parking space, forcing developers to build spaces that sit empty while raising apartment rents. Opponents in outer-borough transit deserts argue that eliminating parking requirements will lead to impossible street congestion. How do we resolve this fundamental geographical divide?

turns.speaker: Dan Garodnick
turns.text: New York City is not a suburban strip mall; we possess the most extensive 24-hour rapid transit network in North America. Today, outdated zoning mandates that a developer building 100 homes near a subway station must construct 50 parking spaces, even if the tenants do not own cars. That parking requirement often makes affordable housing projects physically or financially impossible. Eliminating parking minimums does not ban parking; it allows builders and communities to provide parking based on actual market need rather than rigid government mandates.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Restler
turns.text: Representing Greenpoint, Williamsburg, and Downtown Brooklyn, I strongly support the elimination of parking minimums. We are in a climate emergency and a housing emergency. Mandating parking induces more car ownership, worsens air pollution, and increases carbon emissions, while driving up the construction cost of every single apartment. Cities like Minneapolis, Buffalo, and Austin eliminated parking minimums and saw an immediate acceleration in affordable housing construction without street chaos.

turns.speaker: Alexa Avilés
turns.text: While parking minimum elimination makes sense in transit-rich waterfront districts like Lincoln's, communities like Sunset Park and Red Hook have complex multi-generational households, delivery workers, and small manufacturing businesses that depend on commercial vehicles. If we eliminate parking mandates entirely without investing in bus rapid transit or subway frequency, working-class transit deserts will be left behind.

turns.speaker: Joseph Borelli
turns.text: In the South Shore of Staten Island, there is no subway. The nearest express bus takes two hours to reach Midtown, and families rely on cars to take their children to school, buy groceries, and travel to work. Telling a developer in Staten Island that they don't have to build parking means every new tenant will park their cars on already overcrowded residential streets, sparking endless neighborhood conflict. The Council must reject blanket parking elimination in low-density R1 through R5 zoning districts.

turns.speaker: Justin Brannan
turns.text: Representing Bay Ridge and Southern Brooklyn, I know firsthand the anger parking issues cause. We have to be realistic. A one-size-fits-all policy created in Manhattan does not work in Bay Ridge, Whitestone, or Tottenville. The Council must establish a tiered framework: eliminate parking minimums in the transit-dense urban core, but preserve parking protections or establish transit-distance thresholds in outer-borough low-density districts.

turns.speaker: Gale Brewer
turns.text: Justin's compromise is sensible. In Manhattan Community District 7 on the Upper West Side, parking minimums were eliminated years ago under Manhattan core zoning, and the sky did not fall. But in Queens and the Bronx, where people walk 20 minutes to a bus stop, parking cannot be discarded overnight. We need a targeted approach that respects transit density.

turns.speaker: Kevin Riley
turns.text: The Subcommittee on Zoning is actively negotiating amendments to carve out or modify parking rules for low-density outer-borough districts. We are listening to our colleagues and our constituents.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: We will incorporate a tiered transit-proximity framework for parking mandates into our amendment package. In Round 3, we turn to neighborhood infrastructure and Community Board opposition.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: We open Round 3. During the formal ULURP public review process, 38 of New York City's 59 Community Boards voted to reject or conditionally reject the 'City of Yes' zoning proposal, along with four of the five Borough Boards. Community residents from Queens to Brooklyn have testified that our municipal infrastructure—stormwater sewers, school seats, electrical distribution, and open spaces—cannot absorb tens of thousands of new residents without massive capital investments. How does this Council address these legitimate community objections?

turns.speaker: Charles Barron
turns.text: The community boards are sounding a legitimate alarm that City Hall has ignored for decades. In East New York, we went through a neighborhood upzoning in 2016 under Mayor de Blasio. City Hall promised thousands of affordable homes, new school buildings, and sewer upgrades. What did we get? Market-rate rents increased, real estate speculators bought up brownstones, and the promised infrastructure took eight years to materialize. Until City Hall puts concrete capital dollars into the ground for our sewer systems and schools, we should not pass a single citywide zoning deregulation.

turns.speaker: Vickie Paladino
turns.text: During Hurricane Ida, basements flooded across Queens, and working-class families drowned in illegal basement apartments because the century-old stormwater sewer mains could not handle the runoff. Now City Hall wants to authorize Accessory Dwelling Units and legalize thousands of basement apartments across Queens without spending a nickel on expanding sewer capacity! It is reckless, irresponsible, and dangerous.

turns.speaker: Justin Brannan
turns.text: As Finance Chair, I have drawn a line in the sand with the Mayor's Office of Management and Budget. The City Council will not vote on 'City of Yes' based on verbal promises. We demand a legally binding, front-loaded Capital Infrastructure Commitment Plan funded in the City's Ten-Year Capital Strategy. We are demanding hundreds of millions of dollars for the Department of Environmental Protection's stormwater sewer infrastructure, School Construction Authority seat expansions, and park improvements before a shovel touches the ground.

turns.speaker: Rafael Salamanca Jr.
turns.text: Justin is spot on. If City Hall wants our votes for citywide housing text changes, they must deliver the capital dollars to back it up. We will not allow developers to profit from upzoning while our constituents deal with sewage backups in their basements.

turns.speaker: Dan Garodnick
turns.text: The Administration hears the Council loud and clear. Deputy Mayor Maria Torres-Springer and OMB Director Jacques Jiha are at the negotiating table with Speaker Adams and Chair Brannan right now. We agree that housing growth must be paired with capital infrastructure investment, and we are prepared to formalize a multi-billion-dollar infrastructure commitment agreement with the Council.

turns.speaker: Pierina Sanchez
turns.text: That infrastructure plan must also include money for NYCHA public housing capital repairs. The 400,000 residents living in NYCHA developments face failing boilers, broken elevators, and lead paint. We cannot invest billions in private developer incentives while public housing infrastructure crumbles across the street.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: The Council's leadership has made our terms clear to the Mayor: no capital infrastructure deal, no zoning vote. In Round 4, we examine the final negotiated terms of our $5.0 billion capital and affordability package.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: We convene Round 4. After weeks of intense, round-the-clock negotiations between Council leadership and the Administration, I am proud to announce that we have reached an historic agreement on a landmark $5.0 Billion Capital Infrastructure & Tenant Protection Commitment Package. In exchange for modified zoning text amendments, the Administration has agreed to appropriate $5.0 billion in dedicated capital investments: $2.0 billion for water and sewer infrastructure upgrades, $1.5 billion for NYCHA public housing roof, boiler, and elevator overhauls, $1.0 billion for neighborhood preservation and deep rental subsidies, and $500 million for tenant anti-displacement legal services and eviction defense. Let us review the amended zoning terms.

turns.speaker: Kevin Riley
turns.text: The Land Use and Zoning committees have secured critical structural modifications to the zoning text. First, we have preserved parking mandates in low-density single- and two-family districts outside the transit core, adopting a balanced three-tier geographic framework. Second, we have modified the Accessory Dwelling Unit provision to give local homeowners flexibility while requiring strict DEP stormwater and building safety code compliance. Third, under UAP, we have instituted deep affordability requirements, mandating that projects utilizing city subsidies must include units accessible to families earning 30 percent to 50 percent of AMI.

turns.speaker: Justin Brannan
turns.text: This $5 billion capital package is the largest municipal infrastructure commitment attached to a land use action in New York City history. For the first time, city capital dollars will be tracked through a public, quarterly Council oversight portal with mandatory project milestone reporting from DEP, SCA, and HPD. If the administration fails to obligate the sewer funds, the Council holds the power of the purse in the annual budget adoption.

turns.speaker: Tiffany Cabán
turns.text: The addition of $500 million for tenant anti-displacement, Right to Counsel funding, and code enforcement against predatory landlords is a significant achievement won by progressive advocacy. While I remain skeptical of market-rate upzoning, these resources provide essential shields to protect vulnerable tenants in our districts.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Restler
turns.text: This is a historic compromise. We have modernized 60-year-old exclusionary zoning rules, created a pathway to build 80,000 new homes, and secured $5 billion to fix our sewers, transit, and public housing. This is how responsible progressive government delivers for working people.

turns.speaker: Joseph Borelli
turns.text: Even with $5 billion in spending, this agreement still upzones neighborhoods that do not want it. Throwing billions of taxpayer dollars at sewer pipes does not change the fact that this Council is stripping local community boards of their voice in neighborhood development.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: The amendments are finalized and the capital commitment is signed. In Round 5, we proceed to final floor statements and the roll call vote.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: We are now in Round 5. The clerk will call the roll on Land Use Matter 0118-2024, the 'City of Yes for Housing Opportunity' zoning text amendment, as amended, coupled with the $5.0 Billion Capital Infrastructure & Tenant Protection Agreement. Members may step forward to explain their votes.

turns.speaker: Rafael Salamanca Jr.
turns.text: I vote aye. The Land Use Committee fought tirelessly to ensure that affluent neighborhoods no longer get a pass. With $2 billion dedicated to sewer upgrades and deep affordability guarantees, this modified plan strikes the right balance for working-class New Yorkers.

turns.speaker: Kevin Riley
turns.text: I vote aye. By listening to our communities and amending the parking and density rules, we have delivered a responsible plan that creates homes for our nurses, firefighters, and teachers.

turns.speaker: Keith Powers
turns.text: I vote aye. New York cannot remain an affordable, vibrant global city if we refuse to build homes. This is the most consequential housing action this Council has taken in a generation.

turns.speaker: Justin Brannan
turns.text: I vote aye. We held City Hall accountable and secured $5 billion in real infrastructure dollars for our neighborhoods. Housing without infrastructure is a disaster; housing with infrastructure is the future.

turns.speaker: Pierina Sanchez
turns.text: I vote aye. The dedicated funding for NYCHA and deep affordability tiers ensures that the Bronx will not be left behind.

turns.speaker: Lincoln Restler
turns.text: I vote aye. Decisive action to address our housing emergency, combat exclusionary zoning, and invest in our climate resilience.

turns.speaker: Gale Brewer
turns.text: I vote aye. The modifications secured by Council leadership address the primary concerns of our community boards while allowing our city to grow responsibly.

turns.speaker: Tiffany Cabán
turns.text: I vote aye, with deep reservations. I vote yes solely because of the hard-won $500 million for tenant protections, Right to Counsel, and NYCHA preservation.

turns.speaker: Alexa Avilés
turns.text: I vote no. Market-rate supply-side deregulation will not solve the affordability crisis for families in Sunset Park. We needed mandatory 100 percent affordable housing.

turns.speaker: Charles Barron
turns.text: I vote no. This is another real estate developer plan masquerading as affordable housing. East New York says no.

turns.speaker: Joseph Borelli
turns.text: I vote no. My constituents on Staten Island do not want higher density, traffic congestion, or lost parking. I stand with outer-borough homeowners.

turns.speaker: Vickie Paladino
turns.text: I vote no. This plan destroys our suburban neighborhoods and ignores the unanimous rejection of our Queens community boards.

turns.speaker: Speaker Adrienne Adams
turns.text: I vote aye. By a vote of 31 in the affirmative, 18 in the negative, with 2 abstentions, the 'City of Yes for Housing Opportunity' zoning resolution, as amended, is hereby adopted by the New York City Council. This Council has proven that we can tackle our housing crisis while fiercely defending our neighborhoods, our infrastructure, and our working families. The Stated Meeting is adjourned.
